detailed_rationale:
Cochin Shipyard's order book stood at roughly Rs 21,000-22,300 crore at FY26-end (66% Indian Navy, balance ship repair/commercial), against FY26 revenue of Rs 5,022 crore -- only about 4.3x trailing revenue, a materially thinner multi-year revenue runway than the 'Rs 2.85 lakh crore addressable pipeline' headline number implies. That larger figure is a wish-list of bids/RFIs (IAC-2 second aircraft carrier, next-generation missile vessels/destroyers, export commercial tonnage), not an executable backlog, and the brokerage community has already started discounting it: Kotak Institutional Equities (Sell, target Rs 830, implying ~48% downside from a recent close of Rs 1,595) explicitly flagged 'lack of major defence orders in the last two years,' a near-term pipeline it sizes at just Rs 7,800 crore, and a medium-term pipeline it cut to Rs 30,000 crore from an earlier Rs 50,000 crore estimate. The single largest incremental catalyst -- IAC-2, the second indigenous aircraft carrier, which only Cochin Shipyard can build in India -- has NOT been sanctioned: it still needs Acceptance of Necessity from the Defence Procurement Board, then Defence Acquisition Council clearance, then Cabinet Committee on Security sign-off, with AoN itself only targeted for 'late 2026.' Even if that clears on schedule, INS Vikrant's own build cycle (keel-laid 2009, commissioned 2022) shows aircraft-carrier revenue recognition lags contract award by many years, so IAC-2 is a real, un-calendarable, potentially transformational order -- but not one that can be underwritten in a base-case 3-year model today.

The growth deceleration embedded in the quant snapshot (28.5% 3-year revenue CAGR vs 4.2% trailing 1-year growth) is confirmed against our internal PIT data (our point-in-time quarterly dataset): FY26 quarterly sales printed Rs 1,069cr / 1,119cr / 1,350cr / 1,484cr (Jun/Sep/Dec/Mar), summing to Rs 5,022cr vs FY25's Rs 4,820cr -- a 4.2% full-year increase that badly undershot management's own FY26 guidance of 14-15% revenue growth given on the Q1 FY26 call. This is not primarily a demand problem; it is percentage-of-completion/execution-timing lumpiness inherent to a handful of large fixed-price vessel contracts, and it shows up violently at the quarterly operating-margin level: OPM/EBITDA margin swung from 23% (Jun-25) to just 7%/6.6% (Sep-25) to 14% (Dec-25) back to 21% (Mar-26). The Sep-25 (Q2 FY26) print is the specific earnings-quality flag worth underscoring: net profit fell 43% YoY to Rs 108 crore on a 12% YoY decline in shipbuilding revenue (unfavourable project mix, execution delays, higher sub-contracting cost), and core operations contributed barely Rs 22.6 crore of pre-tax profit against total PBT of Rs 150 crore -- meaning 'other income' (treasury interest plus SBFAP government shipbuilding-subsidy accrual) supplied roughly 85% of that quarter's reported profit. The subsidy accrual itself is delivery-schedule-contingent under SBFAP guidelines -- the company has already had to reverse a portion of previously booked subsidy income (Rs 8.9 crore) in a past period following a revision to expected vessel delivery dates -- so a meaningful slice of reported 'other income' is not a clean, repeatable cash-earnings source but an accounting estimate that can move in either direction with schedule slippage. Separately, Q4 FY26 ship-repair revenue fell 61% YoY (to ~Rs 330cr) purely on a high year-ago base from one-off large repair contracts on INS Vikrant/Vikramaditya -- a reminder that ship-repair, too, is lumpy project-count business, not a smooth annuity, even with the new International Ship Repair Facility (ISRF, operational since August 2024, management guiding to an incremental Rs 250cr in the first 18-24 months scaling to Rs 600cr+ at full utilisation) now ramping.

On valuation, the stock trades at roughly 51-52x trailing earnings (cross-checked independently: FY26 EPS of ~Rs 27.2 -- summing quarterly EPS of 7.14+4.09+5.50+10.51 from the PIT data -- against a current price near Rs 1,390-1,410 gives ~51x, consistent with the quant snapshot's 51.6x despite the snapshot's dated price). That is the richest multiple of the three listed defence shipyards -- Mazagon Dock trades near 39-42x and Garden Reach Shipbuilders (GRSE) near 38-42x -- despite Cochin Shipyard having by far the weakest profitability of the three (ROE ~12-13.6% vs Mazagon Dock's ~37% and GRSE's ~40-41%). Paying the highest multiple in the peer set for the lowest return on equity is difficult to justify on fundamentals alone; the premium is effectively a carrier-optionality/scarcity premium (Cochin is India's only aircraft-carrier-capable yard) layered on top of the broader FY25-26 defence-PSU re-rating wave, most of which has already partly unwound -- the stock is down ~30% over the trailing year and ~9% over six months from a 52-week high of Rs 1,979.90 (low Rs 1,187). The government itself used the recent pullback to sell down a modest stake (2.52% base + 2.52% green-shoe OFS at a Rs 1,400 floor, 7-8 July 2026) as part of its broader FY27 divestment programme -- not alarming in size, but also not a signal of insider conviction that the de-rating has overshot.
recommendation_rationale: This is a genuine, non-trivial judgment call, and I ultimately side with the quant model's Sell rather than override to Hold, though the margin of conviction is narrower than a typical Sell. The case for Sell: growth has decisively decelerated (28.5% 3y CAGR to 4.2% 1y, undershooting management's own 14-15% FY26 guidance), the stock carries the richest multiple (~51-52x trailing) of the three listed defence shipyards while generating the weakest ROE of the three (13.6% vs Mazagon's ~37%, GRSE's ~40%), earnings quality in weak quarters is genuinely thin (Q2 FY26 core operations contributed only Rs 22.6cr of PBT against Rs 150cr reported, the balance from schedule-contingent subsidy accrual and treasury income), FCF yield is negative (-0.13%, heavy ongoing dry-dock/ISRF capex not yet earning a return premium over peers), and at least one large, credible brokerage (Kotak) has moved to an explicit Sell with 48% downside citing a two-year drought in major defence order wins and a lowered medium-term pipeline. The case against a clean Sell, and the reason I flag this for Principal visibility rather than deliver Sell unconditionally: IAC-2 -- the second aircraft carrier, biddable only by this yard -- is a real, un-calendarable, potentially order-book-transforming catalyst sitting inside the analysis horizon (AoN targeted late 2026), sell-side dispersion on this name is unusually wide (Kotak's Rs 830 vs PL Capital's Rs 2,175 -- a ~2.6x spread around a Rs 1,390-1,410 current price, an unusually large disagreement band for the same stock), and a meaningful part of the prior over-valuation has already been worked off via the ~30% 12-month de-rating. On balance the demonstrated pattern -- guidance misses, margin volatility, other-income-propped weak quarters, and a peer-relative multiple unsupported by peer-relative returns -- outweighs the un-confirmed IAC-2 optionality for a base-case call, so Sell stands, but this is close enough, and catalyst-sensitive enough, that it should not be read as a high-conviction Sell.
summary: Cochin Shipyard's FY26 numbers confirm the quant model's read: revenue grew just 4.2% (Rs 5,022cr vs Rs 4,820cr, per internal PIT quarterly data), a sharp step-down from the 28.5% 3-year CAGR and a miss against management's own 14-15% FY26 growth guidance, with quarterly operating margins swinging violently (23% to 7% to 14% to 21% across FY26's four quarters) on percentage-of-completion project-mix timing. The Sep-25 quarter is a genuine earnings-quality flag: net profit fell 43% YoY as core shipbuilding operations generated barely Rs 22.6cr of pre-tax profit, with schedule-contingent SBFAP subsidy accrual and treasury income supplying roughly 85% of that quarter's reported PBT. At ~51-52x trailing earnings the stock is the richest of the three listed defence shipyards despite having by far the weakest ROE (13.6% vs Mazagon Dock's ~37% and GRSE's ~40%), and Kotak has moved to an explicit Sell (target Rs 830, -48%) citing a two-year drought in major defence order wins and a medium-term pipeline it cut to Rs 30,000cr from Rs 50,000cr. Set against that, IAC-2 -- the second aircraft carrier, biddable only by Cochin Shipyard -- remains a real, un-calendarable catalyst (Acceptance of Necessity targeted late 2026, Cabinet Committee on Security sign-off still pending) that could reprice the order book overnight, and brokerage targets are unusually dispersed (Rs 830 to Rs 2,175) after the stock's own ~30% 12-month de-rating. Net call: Sell, but by a narrower margin than the headline multiple alone would suggest, given the live optionality and wide sell-side disagreement.
positive_para: Cochin Shipyard remains India's only aircraft-carrier-capable shipyard, and the Indian Navy is actively moving to secure Cabinet-level approval for IAC-2 (second indigenous aircraft carrier) with Acceptance of Necessity targeted for late 2026 -- a real, if not-yet-sanctioned, order that only this yard can win and that would be transformational for the multi-year order book. The near-term order book of Rs 21,000-22,300 crore (66% Indian Navy) still provides genuine multi-year revenue visibility, including live work on Anti-Submarine Warfare Corvettes and Next Generation Missile Vessels, and the yard continues to win incremental commercial/export business (a Denmark-based contract in the Rs 250-500 crore range, four Azimuthing Stern Drive tug orders via subsidiary Udupi Cochin Shipyard). Two large capacity investments -- the new dry dock and the International Ship Repair Facility (ISRF, operational since August 2024, a Rs 970 crore, 42-acre facility with a 130x25m ship-lift system capable of up to 84 vessels/year) -- are now complete, with management guiding to an incremental Rs 250cr of ISRF revenue in the first 18-24 months scaling toward Rs 600cr+ at full utilisation. Policy tailwinds are genuine and funded rather than merely rhetorical: SBFAP 2.0 (Union Budget FY26) raised the shipbuilding financial-assistance allocation from Rs 4,000 crore to Rs 18,090 crore, alongside a decade-long customs-duty exemption extension on shipbuilding inputs, and the Rs 25,000 crore Maritime Development Fund (announced Budget 2025-26) aims to lift India's global shipping-tonnage share from ~2% toward 5% by 2047 -- a genuine multi-decade structural tailwind for Indian yards' cost competitiveness against Chinese/Korean/Japanese competition. Balance sheet quality is solid for a capital-intensive PSU (D/E 0.28x, interest coverage 8.8x, GREEN balance-sheet flag), and the stock has already absorbed much of the prior defence-PSU re-rating excess, down ~30% over 12 months and ~9% over six months from its 52-week high of Rs 1,979.90 -- some of the valuation risk this desk would otherwise flag has already been worked off by the market itself.
negative_para: Delivered growth has decisively decelerated and undershot management's own guidance: FY26 revenue grew just 4.2% (Rs 5,022cr, confirmed via internal PIT quarterly data) against a 14-15% growth guide given on the Q1 FY26 call and a 28.5% 3-year CAGR base -- and the deceleration is not a smooth glide path but violent quarter-to-quarter execution lumpiness, with operating margin swinging between 6.6% and 28% across the last five reported quarters. The Sep-25 (Q2 FY26) quarter is a genuine earnings-quality concern: net profit fell 43% YoY to Rs 108cr as shipbuilding revenue itself declined 12% YoY on unfavourable project mix and execution delays, and core operations generated barely Rs 22.6cr of the quarter's Rs 150cr pre-tax profit -- the remaining ~85% came from 'other income' (treasury interest plus SBFAP government subsidy accrual), a source that is explicitly schedule-contingent (the company has previously had to reverse Rs 8.9cr of already-booked subsidy income following a vessel-delivery-date revision) rather than a clean, repeatable operating cash flow. Ship-repair revenue fell 61% YoY in Q4 FY26 purely on a high year-ago base (one-off INS Vikrant/Vikramaditya repair contracts), underlining that both shipbuilding and repair revenue are lumpy, contract-count-dependent, not annuity-like. At ~51-52x trailing earnings, Cochin Shipyard is the most expensive of the three listed defence shipyards -- Mazagon Dock trades at ~39-42x, GRSE at ~38-42x -- despite generating the weakest ROE of the three (13.6% vs Mazagon's ~37%, GRSE's ~40-41%) and a negative FCF yield (-0.13%) reflecting heavy ongoing dry-dock/ISRF capex. Kotak Institutional Equities has moved to an explicit Sell (target Rs 830, ~48% downside from a recent Rs 1,595 close), citing a two-year absence of major new defence order wins, a near-term order pipeline it sizes at just Rs 7,800 crore, and a medium-term pipeline cut to Rs 30,000 crore from an earlier Rs 50,000 crore estimate -- i.e., the 'big pipeline' narrative is already being discounted by at least one large brokerage. The Indian government itself used the recent share-price weakness to sell down a modest stake via OFS (2.52% base + 2.52% green-shoe at a Rs 1,400 floor, 7-8 July 2026) as part of its broader FY27 divestment target, adding a modest supply overhang rather than signalling conviction that the de-rating has overshot.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~51-52x trailing earnings, the market is pricing a sustained high-teens-to-20%+ earnings CAGR for a decade-plus (standard reverse-DCF logic: an 11-12% cost of equity with a 6% terminal growth rate needs roughly that trajectory to justify a 50x multiple) -- a bar the company's own recent numbers do not support. FY26 delivered just 4.2% revenue growth against management's own 14-15% guide, the executable order book (Rs 21,000-22,300cr) covers only ~4.3x trailing revenue (thin relative to the multi-year backlogs that typically justify capital-goods premium multiples), and at least one large brokerage now sizes the near-term incremental pipeline at just Rs 7,800cr with the medium-term estimate cut from Rs 50,000cr to Rs 30,000cr. The bull case rests almost entirely on IAC-2 -- a real, sole-source, potentially Rs 40,000-50,000cr+ order -- but that carrier is still pre-Acceptance-of-Necessity (targeted late 2026) with Cabinet Committee on Security sign-off still to come, and INS Vikrant's own history (2009 keel-lay to 2022 commissioning) shows carrier revenue recognition lags contract award by many years even after award. Peer-relative evidence reinforces the stretched read: Mazagon Dock and GRSE, both generating 3x Cochin's ROE (37-41% vs 13.6%), trade 10-15 turns cheaper (39-42x vs 51-52x). My honest judgment is that the current multiple prices in both a IAC-2 award AND clean high-margin execution of the existing book -- neither of which the last four quarters of lumpy, other-income-dependent earnings currently evidences. This is not a name priced for the demonstrated growth/return profile; it is priced for the optionality, and that optionality is not yet contractually real.
escalation_reason: Genuine analytical tension, not a stale-data artefact: (1) sell-side target dispersion on this single name is unusually wide -- Kotak Rs 830 (Sell, -48%) vs PL Capital Rs 2,175 (implied Buy, +55%) against a Rs 1,390-1,410 current price, a ~2.6x spread that signals real disagreement about whether the ~30% 12-month de-rating has already priced in the bad news; (2) IAC-2 (second aircraft carrier, sole-source to this yard) is a live, un-calendarable, potentially order-book-transforming catalyst with Acceptance of Necessity explicitly targeted for late 2026 -- i.e., within the horizon of this review -- that could invalidate a Sell call on short notice, consistent with this desk's standing lesson that defence order wins are gap events, not scheduled ones. Recommend Principal be aware the Sell call could look wrong within a single catalyst window even though the fundamental/valuation case (peer-relative ROE, guidance miss, earnings-quality softness in weak quarters) supports it today. | RESOLVED 2026-07-25: 90%-conviction recheck -> Hold (see recheck_20260725).

technical_commentary: An extraordinary ~16x parabolic run from the 2022 low (136.3) to the 2024 all-time high (2586.4) has been followed by a clear, multi-year corrective downtrend - three consecutive years of lower highs (2586 to 2053 to 1733) with price currently below the 10m/20m averages though still above the longer 40m. A sharp +45% bounce on above-average volume in Apr-26 is a recent constructive sign worth tracking, but the broader structure since the 2024 top remains a correction, not a resumed uptrend.
